host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong New Wave auteur. Both 'Qeysar' and 'Dash Akol' were directed by Masoud Kimiai.

clue_text: In 1978, former Lalehzar dancer and 'Dash Akol' actress Shahrzad stepped behind the camera to direct this, her sole feature film and one of pre-revolutionary Iran's very rare female-directed movies.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: The House Is Black (1962) was directed by Forough Farrokhzad.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: The Night It Rained (1967) was Kamran Shirdel's celebrated mock-documentary.
distractor_rationales.why_wrong: Shirdel directed The Night It Rained, not Shahrzad.

distractor_rationales.why_wrong: Shahid-Saless directed Still Life, whereas Shahrzad directed Maryam va Mani.

explanation: With 'Maryam va Mani' (1978), Kobra Saidi (Shahrzad) became one of the very first Iranian women to write and direct a narrative feature film—just months before the 1979 revolution.

host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong title in the credits. Shahrzad's 1978 directorial feature was 'Maryam va Mani.'

clue_text: Arrested briefly after her 2001 film 'The Hidden Half' explored a young woman's 1979-era leftist past, this prolific Iranian female director also made the feminist box-office hit 'Two Women.'

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: Rakhshan Bani-Etemad is hailed as the First Lady of Iranian Cinema.
distractor_rationales.why_wrong: Bani-Etemad directed 'The May Lady' and 'Under the Skin of the City,' not 'The Hidden Half' or 'Two Women.'

distractor_rationales.why_wrong: Derakhshandeh made social dramas like 'Hush! Girls Don't Scream,' not 'The Hidden Half.'

explanation: Architect-turned-filmmaker Tahmineh Milani became one of post-1979 Iran's most outspoken female directors, drawing both massive audiences for 'Two Women' and brief arrest over 'The Hidden Half.'

clue_text: When the Khatami-era Music Office finally opened the floodgates to licensed pop after 1997, this gravelly-voiced singer—alongside Shadmehr Aghili and Alireza Assar—was credited with recording the Islamic Republic's very first official pop song.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: Mohsen Chavoshi became a massive 2000s rock-pop star.
distractor_rationales.why_wrong: Chavoshi debuted underground in the mid-2000s, nearly a decade after 1997's first permitted pop wave.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: Reza Sadeghi is famed as the 'Man in Black' of Iranian pop.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: Benyamin Bahadori exploded onto the scene in 2006 with 'Donyaye Digeh.'
distractor_rationales.why_wrong: Benyamin belonged to the second wave of post-1997 Iranian pop, not the 1997 pioneer.

explanation: In 1997–1998, Khashayar Etemadi—setting Afshin Yadollahi's and classical lyrics to modern arrangements—launched the first wave of officially permitted pop in post-revolutionary Iran alongside Shadmehr Aghili and Alireza Assar.

distractor_rationales.why_wrong: Bahman Cultural Center is in southern Tehran, whereas the old Rudaki Hall became Talar-e Vahdat.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: Mohammad Esfahani is a celebrated classical-pop tenor.

book_title: Cultural Revolution in Iran: Contemporary Popular Culture in the Islamic Republic
author: Annabelle Sreberny and Massoumeh Torfeh (eds.)
supporting_passage: Alireza Assar's 'Khiaban-khabha' (Street-Sleepers), released in 2001 with an official permit, was later reused by Green Uprising supporters over footage of 2009 protests.

host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong baritone. The singer of 'Khiaban-khabha' ('Street-Sleepers') is Alireza Assar.

clue_text: Surprisingly backed by the Arts Domain (Howzeh-ye Honari), Mohsen Namjoo's sole officially permitted album inside Iran—released in 2007—shared its title with this fragrant Persian citrus fruit and carpet medallion.

distractor_rationales.why_wrong: Namjoo's only officially permitted Iranian release was 2007's Toranj.

host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong album title. Namjoo's sole officially permitted album in Iran was 2007's 'Toranj.'

clue_text: Breaking a major post-1979 stage barrier in 2000, this hugely popular Ershad-licensed pop group became the first official band to feature female backing vocalists and instrumentalists alongside male singers on Iranian stages.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: Kiosk is an unlicensed rock-blues band.

clue_text: Composed by Morteza Neydavoud with lyrics by Malek o-Sho'ara Bahar, this 1927 freedom tasnif—invoking a caged bird lamenting until dawn breaks—became Mohammad Reza Shajarian's signature concert encore.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: Ey Iran is Iran's beloved unofficial national anthem.
distractor_rationales.why_wrong: Ey Iran was composed in 1944 by Ruhollah Khaleqi, not in 1927 by Neydavoud and Bahar.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: Yar-e Dabestani is Iran's iconic student protest song.
distractor_rationales.why_wrong: Yar-e Dabestani dates to 1979–1980, not 1927.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: Bidad is Shajarian's famed 1985 album.
distractor_rationales.why_wrong: Bidad is a dastgah gusheh and 1985 album, not the 1927 Bahar/Neydavoud 'Bird of Dawn' encore.

host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong classic anthem. Bahar and Neydavoud's 'Bird of Dawn' is 'Morgh-e Sahar.'

clue_text: Written in 1944 during the Allied wartime occupation of Iran by lyricist Hossein Gol-e Golab and composer Ruhollah Khaleqi, this stirring march remains Iran's beloved unofficial national anthem.

distractor_rationales.why_wrong: Soroud-e Shahanshahi was the official pre-1979 royal anthem, not Khaleqi's 1944 unofficial anthem.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: Mehr-e Khavaran is the Islamic Republic's official national anthem since 1990.
distractor_rationales.why_wrong: Mehr-e Khavaran was adopted in 1990, forty-six years after 1944.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: Vatanam is a celebrated patriotic song sung by Salar Aghili.
distractor_rationales.why_wrong: Vatanam is a 21st-century piece, whereas Khaleqi and Gol-e Golab wrote 'Ey Iran' in 1944.

explanation: Inspired by witnessing an altercation between an Allied soldier and an Iranian greengrocer in 1944, Hossein Gol-e Golab wrote the lyrics and Ruhollah Khaleqi composed 'Ey Iran'—first sung by Gholam-Hossein Banan.

host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong patriotic march. Khaleqi and Gol-e Golab's 1944 unofficial national anthem is 'Ey Iran.'

clue_text: Originally written by Mansour Tehrani for the post-1979 film 'From Cry to Assassination' and famously sung by Jamshid Jam and Fereydoun Foroughi, this song—meaning 'My Grade-School Friend'—became Iran's universal student protest anthem.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: Mammad Nabudi is the famous 1982 Khorramshahr liberation lament.
distractor_rationales.why_wrong: Mammad Nabudi commemorated the liberation of Khorramshahr during the Iran–Iraq War, not student protests.

distractor_rationales.why_wrong: Iran, Iran was a 1979 revolutionary anthem, not 'My Grade-School Friend.'

distractor_rationales.why_wrong: Koodakaneh is a tender winter/Nowruz nostalgia song, not the student protest anthem.

supporting_passage: The reformist student anthem 'Yar-e dabestani' (My Grade-School Friend), originally written for a 1979–1980 film, became the rallying song of Iranian university protests.

host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong rallying song. Iran's iconic student anthem 'My Grade-School Friend' is 'Yar-e Dabestani-ye Man.'

clue_text: During the 2009 unrest, Mohammad Reza Shajarian set this beloved modern poet's verse 'Zaban-e Atash' ('The Language of Fire') to music, pleading: 'Lay down your gun, for I am disgusted by the language of fire.'

distractor_rationales.why_wrong: Akhavan-Sales wrote 'Zemestan,' which Shajarian also sang, but 'Zaban-e Atash' is by Moshiri.

explanation: Shajarian's 2009 protest piece 'Zaban-e Atash' ('The Language of Fire') put to music Fereydoun Moshiri's poignant anti-violence poem 'Tofangat ra Zamin Bogzar' ('Lay Down Your Gun').

author: Annabelle Sreberny and Massoumeh Torfeh (eds.)
supporting_passage: Shajarian's 'Zaban-e atash' (The Language of Fire), based on contemporary poet Fereydun Moshiri's verse by the same name, directly addresses the perpetrators of violence and asks them to lay down their guns.

host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong modern poet. 'Lay Down Your Gun' ('Zaban-e Atash') was written by Fereydoun Moshiri.

clue_text: Echoing across 1979 street chants, murals, and the mastheads of early revolutionary dailies, the slogan 'Na Sharghi, Na Gharbi' rejected both Cold War superpowers with this famous four-word English phrase.

distractor_rationales.why_wrong: 'Na Sharghi, Na Gharbi' translates literally to 'Neither East, nor West.'

distractor_rationales.why_wrong: 'Woman, Life, Freedom' is 'Zan, Zendegi, Azadi,' not 'Na Sharghi, Na Gharbi.'

distractor_rationales.why_wrong: That chant was 'Esteqlal, Azadi, Jomhuri-ye Eslami,' whereas 'Na Sharghi, Na Gharbi' means 'Neither East, nor West.'

explanation: Chanted in 1979 marches and painted over the Foreign Ministry's gates, 'Na Sharghi, Na Gharbi' ('Neither East, nor West') rejected alignment with either the Soviet bloc or the United States.

host_reactions.wrong_generic: Check your compass. 'Na Sharghi, Na Gharbi' translates to 'Neither East, nor West.'

clue_text: Born in Kerman in 1932, this grande dame of Iranian theater won international acclaim—and France's Legion of Honor—for grand stage adaptations of Rumi, Hafez, Attar, and the Shahnameh.

distractor_rationales.why_wrong: Motamed-Arya is a film star, not the 1932-born theater director of Rumi and Hafez stage epics.

host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong leading lady of the stage. The 1932-born director of Rumi and Shahnameh stage epics was Pari Saberi.

clue_text: Founded in August 1969 under the wing of National Iranian Radio and Television (NIRT), this experimental incubator—known in Persian as 'Kargah-e Namayesh'—nurtured Iran's most daring avant-garde playwrights and directors.

clue_text: Before directing cinema classics like 'Bashu, the Little Stranger,' this towering Iranian playwright and scholar authored the foundational 1965–2000 treatise 'Namayesh dar Iran' ('Performance in Iran').

The conjugal couple was now sartorially distinct from the rest of their families within the scene of marital celebration. Previously, brides and grooms wore fancier clothes, but generally not clothes uniquely marked as wedding clothes or necessarily and uniquely distinct from those of the guests. In Iran, in some aristocratic families, the white European-style wedding dress made its entry by the second decade of the twentieth century. ‘Ayn al-Saltaneh (1872 – 1945), in his memoirs, notes on 5 October 1917 the novelty of two wedding dresses that had been tailored like those in Europe (Farangistan), “white, with a long train on the back that has to be carried by the bride’s maids.”19 The change was uneven and partial, often class-specific. The Achaemenians were enlightened despots who allowed a certain amount of regional autonomy in the form of the satrapy system. A satrapy was an administrative unit, usually organized on a geographical basis. A satrap (governor) administered the region, a general supervised military recruitment and ensured order, and a state secretary kept official records. The general and the state secretary reported directly to the central government. The 20 satrapies were linked by a 2,500kilometer highway, the most impressive stretch being the royal road from Susa to Sardis built by command of Darius I. Relays of mounted couriers could reach the most remote areas in 15 days. As if to remind the satrapies of their limited independence, royal inspectors, the "eyes and ears of the king," would tour the empire and report on local conditions. Inclinations toward restiveness were further discouraged by the existence of the king's personal bodyguard of 10,000 men, called the Immortals. The most common language in the empire was Aramaic. Old Persian was the "official language" but was used only for inscriptions and royal proclamations. Darius I revolutionized the economy by placing it on a system of silver and gold coinage. Trade was extensive, and under the Achaemenians an efficient infrastructure facilitated the exchange of commodities among the far reaches of the empire. As a result of this commercial activity, Persian words for typical items of trade became prevalent throughout the Middle East and eventually entered the English language; examples include asparagus, bazaar, lemon, melon, orange, peach, sash, shawl, spinach, tiara, and turquoise. Trade was one of the empire's main sources of revenue, along with agriculture and tribute. Other accomplishments of Darius's reign included codification of the data, a universal legal system upon which much of later Iranian law would be based, and construction of a new capital at Persepolis, where vassal states would offer their yearly tribute at the festival celebrating the spring equinox. Lacking any domestic source of precious metal coins, Safavid mints in practice functioned primarily by processing – melting and restriking – imported foreign coins. Consequently, the mint suffered if it established a price for a foreign coin which was lower than the market price. Much of the precious metal arriving from the Ottoman Empire came as bullion in the form of silver bars; some was specie, usually either Spanish reals of eight or Dutch rijksdaalders, which were approximately equal in value. On arrival in Iran these were often brought to the mints of Yerevan, Tabriz and Tiflis, to be melted and coined into `abbasis and mahmudis. The seignorage (vajebi) demanded by the state when metal was brought to the mint for coining was partly a tax and partly a fee for minting. With a good excuse a merchant could get a certificate allowing him to take the bullion to Isfahan. But this was not in the interest of the minter who stood to lose his seignorage share. While most of the money entered Iran from the northwest, some came via Basra by caravan from Aleppo. The market price of Iranian coins therefore could not be too far out of line with the market price in Basra. The importance of the local mint of Hoveyzeh in Khuzestan and the concentration of mints in the region in the Safavid period is also explained by the proximity of Basra. The large-scale shipments of specie and bullion to and from Iran made the money supply dependent on factors over which the state had little control. It had survived the Arab conquest without losing its cultural identity, and Persian inﬂuence in culture and administration had been considerable even under Arab rule. Many Iranian languages had survived the conquest: New Persian had become the language of the court, government and literature with the rise of independent states in Iranian lands. And it had so remained even under Turkish and Mongol rulers, in fact becoming the lingua franca for a vast region in western and Central Asia. Yet it was the Safavids who restored the old Persian empire by reuniting virtually the entire Iranian lands as ‘the Protected Kingdoms of Iran’ under one standard, which bore the insignia of the lion holding a sword in its hand and carrying the sun on its back – a Muslim empire, but one which exclusively followed the Twelver Shia faith, once again giving Iran a distinct religious identity. Isma’il was the leader of a fanatical Suﬁ order, and both he and his disciples saw him as a divine being rather than an Iranian nationalist leader. And although the literary and administrative language remained Persian, the Safavids spoke Turkic at court and at home. Large numbers of Armenians have emigrated since the Revolution; in 2000 the Armenian population was estimated at 300,000, about 15 percent less than in 1979. The bulk of the objects are thirteenth century, without apparent effect from the Mongol invasion, but only lustre-painted tiles continue through the first third of the fourteenth century. After about 1340 there is a sudden lack of dated objects until around 1400. Metalwork, on the other hand, seems to have suffered from the invasion from the East. Practically no dated Iranian pieces are known after about 1225 until the latter part of the century when new objects were made for the new masters of the Near East and eventually a distinguishable school was established in southern Iran. Even though it may be assumed that new Iranian metalwork gave, in the twelfth century, a major impetus to Islamic metalwork in general, it is in the Fertile Crescent and Egypt that its greatest thirteenth-century masterpieces will be made. There is one last remark to be made about the techniques. They also, like the monuments of architecture, have regional associations. For metalwork it is quite certain that Khurasan, or, more generally, northeastern Iran, was the main centre from which new techniques derived and in which they were pursued until the Mongol invasion. A separate school has been suggested for north-western Iran, but its existence above the artisanal level is not secure. Ceramics are more difficult to localize properly, but there it would seem clear that the major impetus was in western Iran. Kashan, of course, is the best-known centre and there is no doubt that its potters had acquired a particularly high reputation. The exact significance of the prominence of Kashan for the evaluation of styles and techniques and for the attribution of pieces to specific centres is less easy to determine, for potters from Kashan may indeed have worked elsewhere. distractor_rationales.why_wrong: Dulles championed 'rollback' and global pacts rather than Kennan's selective 'strongpoints.'

explanation: While Kennan's selective 'strongpoints' focused on Western Europe and Japan, NSC-68 and the Korean War elevated Iran into a frontline Cold War domino.
book_title: Mohammad Mosaddeq and the 1953 Coup in Iran
author: Mark J. Gasiorowski & Malcolm Byrne (eds.)
supporting_passage: The more constrained "strongpoints" strategy as described by Kennan and already in use by the United States at the time. Originally, the concept of containing the Soviet Union had entailed reacting to Kremlin aggression anywhere it appeared.

host_reactions.correct_generic: Impressive—the shift from Kennan's selective 'strongpoints' to NSC-68 is what put Iran squarely in the CIA's crosshairs by 1953.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Wrong Cold War strategist—the author of the Long Telegram and 'strongpoints' containment was George Kennan.
